docs.title: Nordhaven: a GPU cloud partner from hardware handover to first workloads
docs.text:
Nordhaven is a fictional European NVIDIA Cloud Partner. It has just received two pools of rented hardware: NVIDIA L4s in Paris (Scaleway) for inference and development, and a 2× H200 SXM5 node with NVLink in Finland (Verda) for training. Its first tenants are a research group that lives in Slurm, a team running distributed PyTorch, and a customer who still ships VMs. This project takes both pools from bare nodes to those tenants with NVIDIA's open stack, from one Git repository, and records why each piece won over its alternatives.

It's Part 2 of my GPU fleet work. Part 1 built Day 2 operations by hand on one L4; here NVIDIA's tools take over, and where Part 1 did the same job, I compare the two on the same GPU model. The AI Factory map shows where these layers sit in a partner's stack.

Both sites run upstream Kubernetes 1.36 through kubeadm, built by the same bootstrap scripts and synced by ArgoCD from the same repository. The two differences come from the providers: Scaleway's L4 boots with no driver, so the GPU Operator installs one, while Verda's image already ships driver 580.178.04, so the operator runs with its driver component off (ADR 0002). The Finland site sends its metrics to Paris as it runs, so they stay queryable after it's deleted. The architecture page covers every component, the network and the sync order.

docs.title: Reading the rest
docs.text:
• What is simulated: every injected fault, simulated GPU and emulated device, in one list. A GPU doesn't fail on request, so the faults were injected.
  • Decisions: one record per real choice, each with at least two alternatives.
  • Findings: what didn't behave as documented.

Names in commands, labels and outputs keep the project's short prefix and site codes: eu1-fin-gpu-01 is the Finland H200 node, par and fin are the Paris and Finland sites, and eu1.io/pool=gpu is a node label. Renaming them would mean redeploying both sites for no technical gain.

docs.title: Day 1: bring a node into service
docs.text: A new GPU node has two questions to answer before a tenant touches it: is it running the right software, and does it actually work? AICR answers the first, NVCRE the second. Both ran on the Paris L4 (21 October 2026) and the Finland 2× H200 node (22 October).

docs.title: AICR: a known-good software stack
docs.text: In shortRun evidence

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A GPU server runs a stack of software on top of the hardware: the driver, the GPU Operator that installs and manages it, monitoring, a scheduler. Each piece has many versions, and not every combination works. A wrong one shows up as GPUs the cluster can't see, or crashes after an upgrade.

docs.title: Two ways to answer "which versions go together?"
docs.text:
Part 1: hand-pinned AICR: locked recipes How I picked each version and checked it against its release notes NVIDIA publishes tested combinations per hardware, OS and platform Output Versions pinned in Git A recipe, rendered as Argo CD apps, plus a validator for a live cluster Trust My reading of the notes NVIDIA's testing

I asked AICR (AI Cluster Runtime, v1.1.0) for both pools and set its answer beside what they run.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
• No recipe fits either pool as built. AICR doesn't know the L4 or kubeadm. For the H200 it has recipes, but all of them require Ubuntu 24.04, and the provider's image is 26.04.
  • Its validator refused the H200 node before checking a single component, on the OS release alone.
  • Most versions still match. GPU Operator, NFD and NVSentinel are the same as AICR's. In two places AICR is behind what I need: cert-manager and Kubeflow Trainer.
  • Its drift check missed a change I made by hand, a controller set back one version. Argo CD reverted the same change in 11 seconds.

docs.title: What I decided
docs.text: AICR is the reference for the H200 pool: the checklist I compare against. It isn't the installer: its bundle would put a second GPU Operator, NFD and Prometheus beside the ones already running. The L4 keeps Part 1's hand-pinned versions, since AICR has nothing for it. Drift detection stays with Argo CD (ADR 0003).

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: I compared Part 1's hand-pinned stack with AICR's locked recipes: AICR is the right reference for a standard H200 pool, but it can't install or validate a cluster that strays from its tested OS, so I use it as a checklist and keep Git as the source of truth.

docs.title: Why the drift check missed it
docs.text: AICR's snapshot keeps one name: tag per image's last path segment. A digest-pinned image has no tag and reads latest, and both pods were named manager, so they merged into one entry. On a GitOps cluster, Argo CD is the drift detector; aicr diff is useful only for what Git doesn't own (OS, kernel, services), once the counters are filtered out.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Nothing was installed from a recipe, so AICR building a cluster isn't shown.
  • The snapshot couldn't read the kernel configuration on either site: neither image ships /boot/config-*.
  • One H200 node is one data point for a recipe meant for fleets. Nothing here was simulated.

docs.title: NVCRE: certify the node before tenants use it
docs.text:
In shortRun evidence

The problem. A new GPU server can arrive broken: a faulty GPU, a slow link between GPUs, a bad driver. If customers land on it first, they find the problem for you.

The idea. Every new server is guilty until proven innocent. It joins the cluster with a "do not enter" sign (a Kubernetes taint, eu1.io/staging), tests run on it, and the sign comes off only if everything passes. That's the gate.

flowchart LR
  join["H200 node joins<br/>taint eu1.io/staging=pending:NoSchedule"] --> cert["NVCRE certification<br/>nccl-all-reduce<br/>nccl-loopback-nvswitch"]
  join --> diag["ECC mode, then dcgmi diag -r 2<br/>as an NVCRE WorkloadRun"]
  cert --> gate["promote.py<br/>every check passed?"]
  diag --> gate
  gate -->|yes| open["taint removed<br/>tenants can schedule"]
  gate -->|no| keep["taint kept<br/>cause: hardware, tooling or unclear"]
flowchart LR
  join["H200 node joins<br/>taint eu1.io/staging=pending:NoSchedule"] --> cert["NVCRE certification<br/>nccl-all-reduce<br/>nccl-loopback-nvswitch"]
  join --> diag["ECC mode, then dcgmi diag -r 2<br/>as an NVCRE WorkloadRun"]
  cert --> gate["promote.py<br/>every check passed?"]
  diag --> gate
  gate -->|yes| open["taint removed<br/>tenants can schedule"]
  gate -->|no| keep["taint kept<br/>cause: hardware, tooling or unclear"]

docs.title: Making NVCRE work on this hardware
docs.text:
NVCRE is built for NVIDIA's standard large servers. Mine are smaller and different, so I changed six things:

NVCRE assumes My reality What I set An H200 server has 8 GPUs Mine is a 2-GPU slice of one gpusPerNode: 2 (1 on the L4) No speed limit: "passed" only means "it ran" I need proof of NVLink A 64 GB/s floor nccl-loopback is the NVLink test That variant switches the GPU-to-GPU path off nccl-loopback-nvswitch, which keeps it on Its hardware test is DCGM level 4 About 90 minutes, on a server billed at $11.66 an hour My own level 2 test, a few minutes Its controller runs away from GPU nodes The docs say so, nothing enforces it A rule that keeps it off GPU nodes Its test pods can enter any node My node carries the "do not enter" sign taintSelectors, so only test pods get in

NVCRE also relies on two things underneath: Kubeflow Trainer, because it launches each test as a training job (a TrainJob), and the DCGM service the GPU Operator runs on every GPU node, which performs the hardware diagnostic.

Why a PyTorch image. The speed test needs NCCL (NVIDIA's library for GPUs exchanging data), CUDA, MPI to launch it across GPUs, and NVIDIA's test program all_reduce_perf_mpi. NVIDIA's PyTorch container ships all of them, tested together. It's also what real training jobs use, so the test exercises the same communication stack customers will.

Driver compatibility. The image (pytorch:26.01) is built for driver 590, and the Finland server runs driver 580. It ran anyway: CUDA 13 programs can run on an older 13.x driver, within limits, and the image also carries its own compatibility libraries. The main test used those; the smaller one used the server's driver directly. I kept pytorch:25.11, built for 580, as a backup. It wasn't needed.

docs.title: What I test, and how
docs.text:
Test Plain English Tool and category Can the GPUs exchange data fast? Training splits work across GPUs, which combine their results after every step (all-reduce). A slow exchange means slow training NVCRE, communication/nccl-all-reduce Are they on the fast road? NVLink is a private bridge, about 450 GB/s each way. PCIe is the shared main road, about 64 GB/s each way NVCRE, communication/nccl-loopback-nvswitch; pass only above 64 GB/s, which only NVLink reaches Is the hardware healthy? Each GPU checks its software, its memory and its PCIe link dcgmi diag -r 2 (DCGM level 2), run as an NVCRE WorkloadRun Is memory protection on? ECC catches and fixes memory errors. With it off, the memory test can't run DCGM field 300 (current ECC mode), read just before the diagnostic

Why the diagnostic runs as a WorkloadRun. A small pod lands on the staged node and asks the node's DCGM service to run the diagnostic. DCGM does the work; the pod is only the messenger, so it needs no special privileges, and it reserves both GPUs so nothing else runs on them meanwhile. I use a WorkloadRun because NVCRE's built-in DCGM test is fixed at level 4, about 90 minutes, and a WorkloadRun is NVCRE's way to run my own test instead. The whole certification stays in NVCRE, with the same entry pass and the same records, rather than me logging into the server.

NVCRE and the gate. NVCRE runs the tests and reports; it never touches the node. My small script, promote.py, reads every result and removes the sign only if everything passed. When it refuses, it says why:

  • Hardware: the node stays out.
  • Tooling: the test itself broke; a person may override, and the override is recorded.
  • Unclear: a person decides. ECC off falls here.

docs.title: What happened on the H200
docs.text:
• The GPUs exchanged data at 351 GB/s: NVLink proven.
  • The diagnostic passed but skipped its memory test, because ECC was off at the provider.
  • The gate let the node in anyway. That was a gap; it now refuses a skipped test and checks ECC first.
  • 19 min 39 s from server ready to open for customers. Part 1's burn-in took 3 hours and ended with a person running a checklist.

Why I didn't turn ECC on. ECC only switches on after a GPU reset or a reboot, and on a rented virtual server the GPUs might not come back. It's also the provider's setting: the fix belongs in the handover spec ("deliver with ECC on"), and my gate's job is to catch it, not to patch the node quietly. So the gate refuses the node as "unclear" and I ask the provider.

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: No node takes customer work until it proves its GPUs talk at NVLink speed and pass NVIDIA's diagnostic, enforced by an automatic gate that says why it refuses. I adapted NVCRE to a 2-GPU server, and the H200 run exposed a blind spot that I then closed.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• NVCRE v0.8.0 and Kubeflow Trainer 2.2.1 on the Finland control plane; the six adaptations are in the "In short" tab.
  • The taint goes on at join, through the node's kubeadm JoinConfiguration, so the node is never schedulable before it's checked. NVCRE never taints, cordons or labels a node; promote.py reads its results file, the diagnostic log and the raw NCCL log.
  • Floor: 64 GB/s bus bandwidth. No published figure exists for two H200s in one node. PCIe Gen5 carries 64 GB/s each way and NVLink about 450 (NVIDIA's H200 page), so above 64 the traffic can only have crossed NVLink. It proves the path, not the performance.
  • Test image nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.01-py3 (built for driver 590), fallback pytorch:25.11-py3 (built for 580), both pinned by digest.

docs.title: Paris L4, 21 October
docs.text: The same gate with gpusPerNode: 1: certified in 1 min 57 s, diagnostic passed in 11 s (memory included, ECC on), promoted at 17:25:54 UTC. Bus bandwidth is 0 with one rank, so this proved the plumbing, not the L4 (report, gate).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Level 2 isn't level 4: no targeted power or stress tests, no nvbandwidth, and on the H200 no memory test.
  • One node: no InfiniBand, RoCE, cross-node NVLink or rack-scale NVSwitch, and no training categories (they need 4 or 32 GPUs).
  • Nothing was simulated; only the Paris L4's taint was added by hand, since that node joins without one.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: A GPU fails in the middle of a training run. Someone has to notice, take the server out of service, move the work, repair the server and bring it back. At 3 a.m. that someone should be software, not a person.

docs.title: Part 1 vs now
docs.text:
Part 1 did this with a controller I wrote. Here NVIDIA's NVSentinel does it, on the same L4 GPU, with the same training job and the same fault (XID 79, "GPU has fallen off the bus"), so the two timelines compare phase by phase.

flowchart LR
  inj["XID 79<br/>in the kernel log"] --> det["Detect<br/>log monitor"]
  det --> q["Quarantine<br/>cordon"]
  q --> d["Drain<br/>evict the job"]
  d --> r["Repair<br/>reboot the node"]
  r --> back["Return<br/>healthy again, uncordon"]
  back --> res["Training resumes<br/>from its checkpoint"]

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
Part 1 NVSentinel Fault to training resumed 360.9 s 288.8 s Goodput (useful share of the run) 66.4% 73.0% People involved One, to approve the return None
  • The waiting disappeared. Part 1 spent 299 s on a safety timer I wrote and about 40 s waiting for a person. NVSentinel detected the fault in 1.3 s and cordoned and drained in 1.7 s more.
  • New work replaced it. NVIDIA's rule for XID 79 is a reboot, which Part 1 skipped. The reboot (115 s) and the driver rebuild after it (123 s) are now 82% of the outage. On a fleet the job would restart on another server about 3 s after the fault.

docs.title: What I had to change
docs.text:
NVSentinel default Why it fails here What I set Drain waits for jobs to finish A training job never finishes on its own, so repair never starts Evict immediately Circuit breaker: stop after 50% of GPU nodes cordoned With one GPU node, the first fault trips it, and it also blocks the return Off here; on a fleet, on with an absolute cap Reboot provider kind Pretends to reboot generic: a real reboot Job MongoDB images from Bitnami amd64 only, so my laptop tests wouldn't match Percona

Part 1's fault injection also needed one fix: the system log stripped the NVRM: tag from the fake line, so NVSentinel couldn't match it. Adding the node's uptime in front, as a real kernel line has and as NVSentinel's own tests do, fixed it.

docs.title: What's still not automated
docs.text:
• No hardware check before the return. The node went back to tenants when the monitors said healthy, without a DCGM diagnostic. NVSentinel can run one (validation after repair); I left it off to measure it as shipped, and I'd turn it on for tenants.
  • Some faults wait for a person by design: those NVIDIA marks "contact support".
  • NVSentinel's brain runs on the Paris CPU worker. When that worker is off, faults are seen but nobody acts.

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: NVSentinel took a GPU fault to resumed training with no human in the loop, 20% faster than my Part 1 controller, and the time left is the reboot NVIDIA prescribes, which a fleet hides by moving the job elsewhere.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• NVSentinel v1.28.0, all three stages on, values in nvsentinel-par.yaml. XID 79 maps to RESTART_BM in NVIDIA's XID catalog, which NVSentinel embeds.

docs.title: Tenancy: sharing scarce GPUs with KAI and MIG
docs.text: In shortRun evidence

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
GPUs never cover demand, so a partner must answer three questions for every customer team (tenant):

  1. How much is guaranteed? A quota no one can take away.
  2. What can be borrowed? Idle GPUs of another team, given back when it needs them.
  3. What about a job that needs several GPUs at once? A distributed training job is useless with half its GPUs: it should start whole or not at all (gang scheduling).

Part 1 only had a fixed cap per team on a shared L4.

docs.title: What I used
docs.text:
• KAI Scheduler (NVIDIA, v0.18.6), on both sites: per-team queues with a guaranteed quota, borrowing, take-back (reclaim) and gangs.
  • MIG (Multi-Instance GPU) on the H200: cuts one GPU into isolated slices, each with its own memory and compute, so two tenants can share one GPU without seeing each other.
Queue Paris (simulated GPUs) Finland (real H200s) team-a quota 4 quota 1 team-b quota 4 quota 1

docs.title: Two lessons
docs.text:
• Two pods on one server don't use NVLink by default. Between the two gang pods, data moved at 2.24 GB/s over the pod network, against 351 GB/s inside one pod holding both GPUs. A tenant's 2-GPU job should run as one pod.
  • KAI won't mix MIG slices and whole GPUs on one server. A pod asking for the second, whole H200 was refused. So a partner splits servers: MIG servers and whole-GPU servers (ADR 0008).

docs.text: Paris's 8 GPUs are fake (two KWOK nodes running no containers). KAI's decisions about them are real. Everything in Finland ran on the real H200s.

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: KAI gave each team a guaranteed share, lent idle GPUs and took them back exactly, never started half a job, and MIG let two tenants share one H200 safely; the run also showed two limits a partner has to design around.

docs.title: HPC: a Slurm group on the same platform, with Slinky
docs.text: In shortRun evidence

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Many research groups have used Slurm, the classic HPC job scheduler, for years. They submit with sbatch and srun and won't rewrite their scripts for Kubernetes. A partner doesn't want a second, separate cluster just for them.

docs.title: What I used
docs.text: Slinky, SchedMD's own operator, runs Slurm inside Kubernetes: Slurm's scheduler and its worker daemons are pods, on the same nodes, monitoring and health checks as every other tenant (ADR 0007 explains why not Soperator or a separate Slurm cluster).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  user["Researcher<br/>sbatch, srun, squeue"] --> login["Login pod"]
  subgraph k8s["Kubernetes cluster, namespace slurm"]
    login --> ctld["slurmctld pod<br/>Slurm's scheduler"]
    ctld --> d0["slurmd pod = Slurm node cpu-0"]
    ctld --> d1["slurmd pod = Slurm node cpu-1"]
    op["Slinky operator"] -->|"creates and keeps<br/>the pods"| ctld
    op --> d0
    op --> d1
    op <-->|"keeps states in sync<br/>(via slurmrestd)"| ctld
  end
  d0 --- node["Kubernetes node<br/>(the Paris CPU worker)"]
  d1 --- node

Slurm keeps its own scheduler and its own idea of "nodes", but every Slurm node is a pod that Kubernetes places, restarts and monitors. The operator is the translator: it keeps Slurm's view and Kubernetes's view of the same machine in agreement.

docs.title: What this shows, beyond "Slurm users can stay"
docs.text:
Adoption is the obvious part. The less obvious part is one operations model for two schedulers:

  • One maintenance switch. An operator, or NVSentinel, marks a machine unusable once, in Kubernetes, and Slurm stops sending it jobs. Without that link, a partner runs two maintenance procedures and Slurm keeps scheduling onto a node Kubernetes already took out.
  • Health checks flow the other way too. Slurm's own pre-job check drains a sick node, and the operator writes Slurm's drain onto the pod as a condition, where the platform's tools look (seen for the cordon drain; for the pre-job drain my capture read the pod too early to show it).
  • One gate, one fleet (designed for GPU nodes). Slurm would only ever see nodes that passed the Day 1 gate, and a GPU node would move between Slurm and KAI by changing a label and a taint, with no second cluster to rebuild.

docs.title: Maintenance: Kubernetes, NVSentinel and Slurm together
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  fault["GPU fault (XID)"] --> nvs["NVSentinel<br/>cordons the Kubernetes node"]
  admin["Planned maintenance<br/>kubectl cordon"] --> cordon["Kubernetes node cordoned"]
  nvs --> cordon
  cordon -->|"Slinky: Node was cordoned"| sdrain["Slurm node drained<br/>no new jobs"]
  podc["Pod-level cordon<br/>annotation on one slurmd pod"] -->|"shown: 6 s"| sdrain
  nvs --> evict["NVSentinel evicts the pods,<br/>slurmd included"]
  evict --> reboot["Reboot, health back,<br/>uncordon"]
  reboot --> resume["slurmd pod returns,<br/>Slurm node back to idle"]
  prolog["Slurm pre-job check fails"] -->|"shown: 1 s"| sdrain2["Slurm drains the node,<br/>holds the job"]
  sdrain2 -.->|"operator mirrors it"| podcond["Pod condition<br/>SlurmNodeStateDrain"]
Link Status Pod cordon in Kubernetes drains the Slurm node Shown, 6 s, and undone 6 s after the annotation is removed Slurm's pre-job check drains a sick node and holds the job Shown, 1 s; the job completed once the node was fixed. The pod condition for this drain wasn't captured Node cordon (by a person or NVSentinel) drains the Slurm node Same operator code path (syncCordon), not run here NVSentinel on a Slurm GPU node Designed, not run: the Paris Slurm is CPU only. NVSentinel evicts per namespace, here Immediate for every tenant, so the slurmd pod goes with the reboot. For a hard fault like XID 79 the job is already dead; for softer faults a partner would let Slurm's drain finish first

Check Result A user's jobs srun across both Slurm nodes and an sbatch job completed in 7 s A health check before every job A sick node (simulated fault) was drained by Slurm in 1 s; the job was held, then completed once the node was fixed Kubernetes and Slurm agree on maintenance Cordoning a worker pod in Kubernetes drained the matching Slurm node in 6 s

One upstream bug: Slinky's default update mode undid that drain one second later. I switched to the mode that holds it, at the price of a manual step per node on upgrades.

docs.title: Slurm with GPUs: designed, not run
docs.text:
Running it would have meant untested work on a rented H200, so I wrote the design instead:

  • Whole GPUs work with the standard Slurm image; MIG slices and a GPU health check need a custom image (built with NVIDIA's NVML library).
  • Each GPU server belongs either to Slurm or to KAI, never shared: a label and a taint keep them apart, and Slurm's pod takes every GPU on its server.
  • The same certification gate applies: Slurm only sees a server after it passed Day 1.
  • Tenants bring their own container (pyxis), so their CUDA version stays their choice, within the driver's limit.

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: Slurm users keep sbatch, while the partner runs one platform where a single cordon, by a person or by NVSentinel, also drains Slurm, and Slurm's own health checks show up in Kubernetes; the GPU version is designed on paper.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• One Application, slinky: slurm-operator and slurm charts 1.2.3, Slurm 26.05, in namespace slurm on the Paris CPU worker. Two Slurm nodes (cpu-0, cpu-1) on one VM (oversubscribeNode); slurmctld state on a 2 GiB local-path volume.
  • Keys made in the cluster, not in Git: the chart's randAscii + lookup would change on every Argo CD sync (finding), so a wave -1 Job creates the auth and JWT keys once, as immutable Secrets.
  • Prolog 00-node-health.sh: fails if /tmp isn't writable, if under 256 MiB of memory is free, or if the SIMULATED marker /var/run/eu1-simulated-fault exists.
  • No accounting (no slurmdbd), no ssh logins (sssd not wired): the test runs commands in the login pod.

docs.title: Slurm with GPUs, Finland: designed, not run
docs.text:
Written from the source at the pinned versions (slurm-operator and chart 1.2.3, Slurm 26.05.5, GPU Operator v26.7.2, KAI v0.18.6); only helm template was run.

nodesets:
  h200:
    enabled: true
    replicas: 1                      # one slurmd pod per GPU node
    slurmd:
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 2          # every GPU on the node
    extraConfMap:
      Gres: ["gpu:2"]                # becomes slurmd -Z --conf "Gres=gpu:2"
    updateStrategy:
      type: OnDelete                 # as in Paris, so a pod-cordon drain holds
    podSpec:
      nodeSelector:
        eu1.io/pool: gpu-slurm
      tolerations:
        - key: eu1.io/slurm
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
controller:
  extraConfMap:
    GresTypes: [gpu]
configFiles:
  gres.conf: |
    AutoDetect=nvidia
  cgroup.conf: |
    CgroupPlugin=cgroup/v2
    IgnoreSystemd=yes
    ConstrainDevices=yes             # a job sees only the GPUs Slurm gave it
Topic Design From the source GPUs into slurmd Via the device plugin and NVIDIA runtime; ConstrainDevices fences each job The chart enables DCGM for any NodeSet with an nvidia.com/gpu limit GRES On the NodeSet, not a NodeName= line Slinky starts slurmd as a dynamic node, slurmd -Z --conf Whole GPUs vs MIG AutoDetect=nvidia works for whole GPUs; MIG needs AutoDetect=nvml, so an image rebuilt with NVML The pinned slurmd image has gpu_nvidia.so, no gpu_nvml.so GPU health check Prolog dcgmi diag -r 1 via Service nvidia-dcgm:5555 (node-local); needs dcgmi in the image and a UUID map of GPU indices GPU Operator v26.7.2 assets/state-dcgm/0500_service.yaml KAI vs Slurm Per node: label eu1.io/pool: gpu-slurm, taint eu1.io/slurm; slurmd takes every GPU; the staging taint applies to both Slinky's workload-isolation guide Faults NVSentinel cordons the node, Slinky drains the Slurm node syncCordon holds under any update strategy CUDA Tenants bring their container through pyxis; the platform publishes the driver ceiling (CUDA 13.0 native on 580) Slinky's pyxis guide runs the login container privileged

Not run because every minute is a rented H200, and no check without a GPU reaches what matters: whether AutoDetect finds the GPUs in the pod, whether ConstrainDevices fences them, whether the prolog reaches DCGM.

docs.text:
• Two Slurm nodes on one VM; no shared storage; no accounting or fair share over time.
  • The Paris Slurm is CPU only. Not compared with a bare-metal Slurm.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Operators need one place to see every GPU of both sites. The Finland site only exists while its H200s are rented, so its metrics must stay readable after the site is deleted.

docs.text:

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• Asking about a deleted site needs a look back. A "now" query sees nothing 5 minutes after the last sample; queries and dashboards have to cover the run's time.

  • Capacity: 40 to 51 series per GPU means 400,000 to 510,000 series for 10,000 GPUs, before pod churn: arithmetic from three GPUs, not a load test.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Some customers can't move to containers yet: they ship a whole operating system, a licensed appliance, or software that expects its own kernel. A partner wants to sell them capacity from the same fleet, run by the same people and tools, instead of running a second platform for VMs.

docs.title: What I used
docs.text: KubeVirt runs a virtual machine as a Kubernetes object: Argo CD deploys it, a tenant quota limits it, the same scheduler places it. The VM uses the server's hardware virtualisation (KVM), not slow software emulation (ADR 0010 explains why not a separate IaaS).

docs.title: What I had to change
docs.text:
• The operator demands a control-plane node; I moved it to the worker.
  • Argo CD can't tell when KubeVirt is ready, so a hook waits before creating the VM.
  • Pinning the operator's image doesn't pin the 13 components it deploys; each one is pinned explicitly.

Designed and checked without a GPU; not run yet. Nothing on this page has served a request. The deployment is prepared for Dynamo v1.5.1 and waits for a run on the Paris L4.

In shortRun evidence

docs.title: Why inference matters to a partner
docs.text: Training fills GPUs in large blocks for weeks. Inference is the steady business: every chat, search or agent call is a request that must answer fast. A partner that only rents GPU hours competes on price; a partner that serves tokens competes on latency, throughput and cost per token, and those depend on how the serving layer uses the GPUs.

docs.title: The problems Dynamo addresses
docs.text: Problem What goes wrong without it What Dynamo does Prefill and decode fight on the same GPU Reading a long prompt (prefill) is compute-heavy; generating tokens one by one (decode) is memory-bandwidth-heavy. On one GPU, a long prompt stalls everyone's token stream Runs them as separate worker pools (disaggregated serving), each sized and scaled on its own The same prompt prefix is recomputed System prompts and multi-turn chats repeat the same opening; each worker rebuilds the same KV cache A KV-cache-aware router sends a request to the worker that already holds its prefix KV cache outgrows GPU memory Fewer concurrent sessions fit in HBM; old context is thrown away and recomputed The KV Block Manager moves cache blocks down to CPU memory or storage and back Moving KV cache between GPUs is slow Disaggregation only pays if prefill can hand its cache to decode quickly NIXL transfers it over the fastest path: NVLink inside a server, RDMA between servers Traffic changes all day Fixed pools either waste GPUs or miss latency targets The Planner scales prefill and decode workers against latency targets

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  client["Client<br/>OpenAI-compatible API"] --> fe["Frontend<br/>HTTP, tokenisation"]
  fe --> router["Router<br/>KV-cache-aware"]
  router --> prefill["Prefill workers<br/>vLLM, SGLang or TRT-LLM"]
  router --> decode["Decode workers"]
  prefill -- "KV cache via NIXL<br/>NVLink or RDMA" --> decode
  decode --- kvbm["KV Block Manager<br/>GPU, CPU memory, storage"]
  planner["Planner<br/>scales the pools"] -.-> prefill
  planner -.-> decode
  subgraph k8s["On Kubernetes"]
    op["Dynamo operator<br/>DynamoGraphDeployment"]
    sched["KAI Scheduler, Grove<br/>gangs and topology"]
  end
  op -.-> fe
  op -.-> prefill
  op -.-> decode
  sched -.-> prefill
  • One object describes the service. A DynamoGraphDeployment lists the components (frontend, workers, prefill, decode, planner) and the operator creates the pods.
  • Backend-agnostic. The worker runs vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM; clients only see an OpenAI-compatible API, so existing applications work unchanged.
  • Fits the platform already built. Pods can be scheduled by KAI in a tenant's queue, and a component can carry a topology constraint, so prefill and decode land where NVLink or the fabric connects them.

docs.title: What it gives a partner like Nordhaven
docs.text:
• Sell inference, not only GPU hours: a managed, OpenAI-compatible endpoint per tenant, on the same fleet, quotas and monitoring as training.
  • More tokens per GPU, so a lower cost per token: prefix reuse and disaggregation remove repeated and interfering work.
  • Latency tiers: separate prefill and decode pools, scaled against latency targets, let a partner sell different service levels.
  • Use of the fabric it paid for: KV cache moves over NVLink and RDMA, so the Spectrum-X or InfiniBand investment serves inference too.
  • Mapped onto Nordhaven's pools: aggregated serving of small models on the Paris L4s; disaggregated prefill and decode across the two NVLink-connected H200s in Finland.

docs.title: In one sentence
docs.text: Dynamo turns GPUs into an inference service: it splits prompt reading from token generation, reuses and moves KV cache over NVLink and RDMA, and scales each part to latency targets, which lets a partner sell tokens at a lower cost per token instead of raw GPU hours.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Two sites, two providers, one repository. Paris stays up between GPU runs: a small control plane and a CPU worker that I power off when nothing needs it, plus an L4 node created for a GPU run and destroyed after. The whole Finland site, control plane included, exists only while I rent its H200 node. Everything that runs in either cluster comes from ArgoCD reading main; a person runs terraform through make, and git push.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  admin["Admin IP ranges"]

  subgraph paris["Paris: Scaleway security groups, inbound drop by default"]
    direction TB
    pcp["Control plane<br/>22 and 6443 from admin ranges"]
    pcpu["CPU worker<br/>22 from admin ranges<br/>30291 from the Finland nodes only"]
    pgpu["L4 node<br/>22 from admin ranges"]
    pn["Scaleway Private Network<br/>node to node, Flannel VXLAN"]
    pcp --- pn
    pcpu --- pn
    pgpu --- pn
  end

  subgraph finland["Finland: nftables on each node, no cloud firewall"]
    direction TB
    fcp["Control plane<br/>22 and 6443 from admin ranges"]
    fgpu["H200 node<br/>22 from admin ranges"]
    fcp <-->|"everything, peer address only"| fgpu
  end

  admin --> pcp
  admin --> fcp
  fcp -->|"Prometheus remote write<br/>mutual TLS, tenant from the client cert"| pcpu

Paris's nodes talk over a Scaleway Private Network, and only SSH and the API server face the admin ranges. Verda has no private network or cloud firewall, so each Finland node runs nftables: SSH and the API server from the admin ranges, everything from the other node's address, nothing else. The one path between sites is Finland's Prometheus writing to Thanos Receive on NodePort 30291 of Paris's CPU worker. The security group opens that port to the Finland control plane when it's created, adds the H200 node's address when that joins, and closes it when the site is deleted. Receive accepts only client certificates signed by its own CA, and takes the tenant (fin) from the certificate's common name, so a Finland series can't claim to be from Paris.

docs.title: GitOps
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  main["main branch"]
  subgraph per_site["each site's ArgoCD"]
    root["root Application<br/>gitops/sites/<site>/root.yaml"]
    base["gitops/apps/<site>/base/<br/>the platform"]
    uc["gitops/apps/<site>/{readiness,scheduling,platform}/<br/>one folder per area"]
    root --> base
    root --> uc
  end
  main --> root

Each site's ArgoCD holds one root Application that reads gitops/apps/<site>/ recursively: an app-of-apps. Only Application manifests live there; the manifests and Helm values they point at sit in gitops/manifests/ and gitops/values/. Shared charts read a base values file, then a per-site file, then one file per area if it exists, so each area changes a shared chart by adding its own overlay instead of editing the base.

Sync waves order the platform on Paris: storage and the object-store credentials at -1, NFD and kube-prometheus-stack at 0, the GPU Operator at 1, cert-manager at 3, tenant namespaces at 4, Garage at 5, and everything else at 10 or later. Finland uses the same waves for the subset it runs. ArgoCD needs the Application health check in argocd-cm for waves to hold across an app-of-apps, as Part 1 found; both sites set it at bootstrap.

docs.title: How the use cases connect
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  join["GPU node joins<br/>with eu1.io/staging taint"]
  accept["Acceptance<br/>cuda-vectoradd, nvidia-smi"]
  cert["NVCRE certification<br/>NCCL all-reduce"]
  diag["dcgmi diag -r 2<br/>ECC checked first"]
  gate{"promotion gate"}
  tenants["Tenants scheduled<br/>KAI queues, gangs, MIG"]
  watch["DCGM and kernel log<br/>metrics to Thanos"]
  fault["NVSentinel<br/>cordon, drain, reboot"]

  join --> accept --> cert --> diag --> gate
  gate -->|"taint removed"| tenants
  gate -->|"refused"| join
  tenants --> watch
  watch -->|"XID 79"| fault
  fault -->|"healthy again"| tenants

A new node is useless to tenants until the gate removes its staging taint: only the GPU Operator, NFD, the acceptance pods and NVCRE's jobs tolerate it. After promotion, KAI places tenant pods from per-team queues, DCGM's series flow into Thanos, and NVSentinel watches for faults. A node it drains comes back through the same health check before it takes work again.

docs.title: What one site or one GPU can't show
docs.text:
• NVLink across nodes, InfiniBand, NVSwitch fabrics. The H200 node has two GPUs linked by NVLink inside one machine; nothing here spans machines at GPU speed.
  • Two real GPU sites at once. The two GPU runs were a day apart, so the cross-site dashboard shows the L4 and the H200 from different times, never side by side live.
  • Scale. One L4 and two H200s exercise every control path, not the load of a fleet.

docs.title: ADR 0001: Two sites on two providers, one repository
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: both sites, the bootstrap and GitOps layout. Use case: all.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Nordhaven has two pools with different jobs: L4s for inference and development, and H200s with NVLink for training. A real partner rarely gets both from one building, and what usually differs between its sites is the layer underneath: networking, firewalls, images, who installs the driver. I wanted the project to meet those differences rather than avoid them, while keeping one way to bootstrap and operate both pools. Cost decides the rest: the H200s can only exist while they're in use.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. One site, one provider Both pools on Scaleway in Paris, one cluster One network, one firewall model, one bill. Part 1's setup almost unchanged The bootstrap and GitOps never meet a second provider, which is the part a multi-site partner actually has to solve. Nothing about metrics or readiness has to cross a site boundary B. Two sites, two providers, one repository Paris on Scaleway (L4, persistent control plane), Finland on Verda (2× H200 SXM5), each a kubeadm cluster with its own ArgoCD reading the same repository The same scripts, versions and Git layout on both; the provider differences show up as small, named overlays. Verda rents a 2× H200 NVLink node by the hour, billed in 10-minute blocks Two firewall models, two image catalogs, metrics that cross the internet, and a site that has to be built from zero in minutes every time C. One cluster stretched across both sites A single control plane in Paris, the H200 node joining over the internet One API, one scheduler view of every GPU Kubelet, etcd-adjacent traffic and the pod network over the public internet; a Paris outage stops Finland's training. No partner would run a production cluster like this

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
B. Each site is its own cluster, both built by the same bootstrap from the same repository, with the provider differences kept in per-site files: terraform/par and terraform/fin, gitops/apps/par and gitops/apps/fin, and -par/-fin values overlays. The one thing that crosses sites is metrics, over Thanos remote write with mutual TLS (ADR 0009).

This would change for a partner whose sites share a private backbone: then a single metrics store without remote write, or even a stretched cluster for CPU-only services, becomes reasonable.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Verda has no private network and no cloud firewall, so the Finland nodes run nftables from their startup script; Paris uses Scaleway security groups and a Private Network. Same bootstrap, two firewall paths.
  • The provider decides who installs the GPU driver on each site, and the two sites end up on different driver branches (ADR 0002).
  • The Finland site is rebuilt from nothing for every GPU run. On 22 October its control plane came up in about 3.5 minutes and the H200 node went from order to two schedulable GPUs in 2 minutes 49 seconds.
  • Capacity isn't guaranteed. At 11:19 Paris on 22 October Verda had no H200 of any size in any location; one appeared in FIN-02 at 11:46. A partner plans around the same problem with reservations; here a poll and a pre-approved spot fallback stood in.
  • Two bootstrap paths mean two sets of bugs. Two of them only showed on the real H200 run, because the CPU-only tests of the Finland site skip those code paths (findings).

docs.title: ADR 0002: Who owns the GPU driver: the GPU Operator or the provider image
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: GPU driver lifecycle on both sites. Use cases: 1, 2.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Part 1's main result was a driver that comes from Git: the L4 boots with no driver, the GPU Operator installs the version pinned in its values, and an upgrade is a commit. Verda's GPU images arrive with a driver already installed and loaded. "Ubuntu 26.04 + CUDA 13.4 Open" (26.04.cuda13.4) ships 580.178.04, from the R580 server branch, while Paris runs 595.91.07. Whoever installs the driver also owns its upgrades, its kernel module builds and the blame when they break, so this has to be decided per site, not per cluster component.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. GPU Operator everywhere Boot a driverless image on Finland too (26.04.base) and let the operator build 595.91.07 there One driver branch and one upgrade path on both sites, from Git Never tested on Verda's H200 VMs, and the first test would cost H200 time: a driver container building against kernel 7.0 on a passthrough VM, with fabric-manager questions on an NVLink machine. The provider supports its own image on that hardware, not mine B. Provider image everywhere Use each provider's GPU image and turn the operator's driver off on both sites No driver build on any node Scaleway's L4 path in Part 1 had no driver in the image, and moving Paris off the operator gives up the driver-from-Git result Part 1 was built on C. Per site: the owner of the image owns the driver Paris: the operator installs 595.91.07 from Git. Finland: the image's 580.178.04, with driver.enabled=false and the packages held Each driver stays with whoever supports it on that hardware; no H200 time spent on driver builds Two branches in one fleet: CUDA images and tests must suit 580 on Finland D. Upgrade the provider's driver by hand Keep Verda's image and install 595 over it at boot One branch A driver nobody owns: neither Git nor the provider. That's the drift Part 1 set out to remove

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
C. The owner of the image owns the driver, and the driver owner picks the branch. On Paris the GPU Operator installs 595.91.07, pinned in gitops/values/base/gpu-operator-par.yaml. On Finland the operator runs with its driver component off, the bootstrap fails within a minute of boot if the image's driver doesn't see both GPUs, and it holds the NVIDIA packages with apt-mark hold so nothing upgrades them during a run.

I'd revisit A if Verda published a driverless H200 image it supports, or if Nordhaven needed one driver branch across the fleet for a certification or a support contract.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Two driver branches in one fleet. Anything built for a newer driver has to be checked against 580 on Finland. NVCRE's pytorch:26.01-py3 image ran there through CUDA compatibility; how it did is in the findings.
  • The acceptance test on Finland checks the driver the image reported at boot, not a version in Git. Paris's check compares against Git, as in Part 1.
  • AICR's H200 recipe assumes its own driver and OS choices; the comparison is on the Day 1 page.
  • On the H200 node the provider's choices come along with its driver. On 22 October ECC was off on both GPUs, which the readiness gate now refuses (ADR 0004).

docs.title: ADR 0003: AICR as the known-good reference for the H200 pool, hand-pinned values for the L4
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: GPU stack versions, Finland H200 pool and Paris L4 pool. Decided after the H200 run, 22 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Nordhaven needs one answer per hardware class to "which versions of the GPU stack go together": operator, driver, DCGM, NFD, scheduler, monitoring. Part 1 pinned each version by hand in Git and checked them against each component's release notes. NVIDIA's AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) generates version-locked recipes per service, accelerator, OS and intent, renders them for Argo CD, and validates a cluster against them. Nordhaven's two pools are a 2× H200 node on Verda in Finland and an L4 on Scaleway in Paris, both on self-managed kubeadm.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. AICR v1.1.0 deploys the H200 pool Its Argo CD bundle replaces the Finland site's base platform One NVIDIA-tested set of versions, installed as tested No recipe matches the Finland node (below); the bundle brings a second GPU Operator, NFD and Prometheus next to the base platform's, plus KAI, the DRA driver and NodeWright, all of which would have to be reconciled with what already runs there B. AICR as the reference, hand-pinned values deploy The Finland site keeps its base platform; AICR's recipe is rendered and kept, compared version by version, and aicr validate runs against the live cluster The known-good set is NVIDIA's, the deployment stays one Argo CD tree Nordhaven already runs and understands Two sources of versions to keep in step by hand; drift between them is a review task, not a sync C. Hand-pinned only, as in Part 1 Each version pinned and checked against release notes No new tool Every combination is Nordhaven's own research, per hardware class

AICR at v1.1.0 doesn't have a recipe for what Nordhaven runs, which is what limits option A:

Query (aicr recipe ...) Result --service kubeadm --accelerator h200 Refused: invalid service type: kubeadm --service generic --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training Refused: generic exists for self-managed clusters but only with GB300 --service metal3, kind, bcm with H200, Ubuntu, training Refused: no such recipe --service eks or k0s with H200, Ubuntu, training Resolves; k0s is the only one that leaves the driver to the host, as Verda's image does, but its container toolkit points at k0s's containerd --accelerator l4 with any service Refused: invalid accelerator type: l4 Every recipe that resolves Constrains Ubuntu to 24.04; the Finland image is 26.04

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
B for the H200 pool, C for the L4. AICR's recipe is the reference that the Finland versions are checked against, and aicr validate runs against the Finland node; nothing from the bundle syncs. The L4 keeps Part 1's hand-pinned values, with AICR's resolved versions as the reference where the two overlap, because AICR covers neither the L4 nor kubeadm.

What would change it: a kubeadm or generic H200 recipe, or Ubuntu 26.04 support, would make A worth a trial; an L4 entry would bring the Paris pool under the same reference.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Where the Finland pool and the reference stand (its versions from the Argo CD Applications in Git; AICR's from the k0s H200 training recipe):

Component AICR v1.1.0 Finland Action GPU Operator v26.7.2 v26.7.2 Aligned NFD 0.19.0 0.19.0 Aligned Driver host-owned in the k0s recipe (the eks one pins 580.173.02) 580.178.04, from Verda's image Same branch, newer patch; ADR 0002 owns the driver kube-prometheus-stack 84.4.0 91.4.1 Newer here; kept, since the cross-site metrics rely on it cert-manager v1.20.2 not in Finland; v1.21.2 in Paris AICR's pin is below the 1.21 that NVSentinel v1.28.0's README asks for NVSentinel v1.28.0 not in Finland; v1.28.0 in Paris Aligned where it runs KAI Scheduler v0.16.9 v0.18.6 Chosen in ADR 0006 Kubeflow Trainer 2.2.0, namespace kubeflow (the eks Kubeflow recipe) 2.2.1, kubeflow-system NVCRE v0.8.0 needs exactly 2.2.1; AICR's would break it DRA driver, NodeWright, prometheus-adapter 0.5.0, v0.20.0, 5.3.0 not deployed Out of scope for this PoC

In Paris it missed a hand-made version change (NVCRE v0.8.0 to v0.7.0): its snapshot keeps one name: tag per image's last path segment, so a digest-pinned image reads latest, and real changes are buried in runtime counters. Argo CD found and undid the same change in 11 seconds. AICR's snapshot stays useful for what Git doesn't own (OS, kernel, services), once the counters are filtered.

docs.title: ADR 0004: NVCRE certification behind a staging taint as the readiness gate
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: readiness gate for new GPU nodes, Finland H200 pool (tested on the Paris L4 too). Decided after the H200 run, 22 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A GPU node Nordhaven receives from a provider shouldn't take a tenant's job until something has shown it works: GPUs talk to each other at the speed the hardware promises, and the diagnostic finds nothing. Part 1 proved an L4 with burn-in scripts and a runbook that a person ran; nothing stopped a tenant scheduling there in the meantime. Nordhaven's training pool is 2× H200 per node, rented by the hour, so the check has to be short, and it has to block scheduling until it passes.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. NVCRE v0.8.0 behind a staging taint NVIDIA's Cluster Readiness Engine runs catalog categories (NCCL collectives, NVLink loopback, DCGM level 4, training) as TrainJobs and writes a results file; the node joins tainted and a small gate removes the taint on a pass NVIDIA's own sizing and NCCL tuning per architecture; one results format for every pool and site; multi-node categories ready for when Nordhaven has more than one node; tolerations injected for the staging taint Doesn't fit a 2-GPU H200 or an L4 out of the box (gpusPerNode, no L4 entry); ships no thresholds; its only DCGM category runs about 90 minutes; never taints or promotes, so the gate is mine; releases weekly B. Part 1's burn-in and runbook dcgmi diag -r 3, three hours of tensor load, a stability record, and a handover checklist run by a person Proven on the L4, criteria written before the run, catches thermal and stability faults a short test misses A person in the loop, three hours per node, nothing blocks scheduling while it runs, no interconnect test at all C. My own gate from upstream tools A Job running nccl-tests' all_reduce_perf and dcgmi diag, and a script reading their output Small, no CRDs, exactly the categories I want I'd own per-architecture sizing and NCCL settings, the output parsing and a results format, for every GPU type Nordhaven adds

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A, with two additions of mine: the staging taint at join, and dcgmi diag -r 2 beside the certification, because NVCRE's DCGM category is level 4 only and 90 minutes is too long for a node billing by the hour while it waits. What decided it is that NVCRE carries the per-architecture knowledge (GPUs per node, NCCL environment, which loopback variant crosses NVLink) that option C would make me maintain, and that its results file is the same on every site, which is what a gate needs to read.

What would change it: a provider that hands over nodes already certified with NVCRE's level 4 would let Nordhaven trust their report and keep only the short checks; and if NVCRE's catalog ever gets a shorter DCGM level, the diagnostic moves inside it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The gate is code Nordhaven owns (scripts/readiness/promote.py, tested), because NVCRE deliberately leaves promotion to the platform. It tells hardware from tooling failures, so a broken test doesn't get read as a broken GPU.
  • Thresholds are Nordhaven's to set and justify. Without one, PASSED only means "ran". In Finland the floor is 64 GB/s bus bandwidth, the most PCIe Gen5 can carry each way, which proves NVLink without pretending to be a performance target.
  • Level 2 isn't level 4: no targeted power, no targeted stress, no nvbandwidth. The use case 2 page says what was skipped.
  • What one node can't show: the inter-node fabric and rack-scale NVLink that NVCRE's multi-node categories are built for, and the training categories (4 GPUs at least).

docs.title: What the runs showed
docs.text:
The gate worked as designed on both sites. The Finland 2× H200 node went from Ready to open in 19 min 39 s on 22 October, certified at 351 GB/s all-reduce bus bandwidth over NVLink, and the same gate ran on the Paris L4 the day before. Two things changed the gate:

  • A skipped test passed. ECC is off on Verda's H200s, so DCGM skipped its memory test and still reported PASS, and the gate, which trusted DCGM's overall result, opened the node with no memory check. The gate now refuses with cause "unclear" when DCGM skips any test, and the diagnostic first records each GPU's current ECC mode (DCGM field 300, read from the same host engine); a GPU with ECC off is refused as "unclear", and a missing record as "tooling". Fed the H200's diagnostic log unchanged, the gate now refuses that node. The ECC read itself hasn't run on a GPU yet.
  • NVCRE's summary can't be the record of the transport. It printed Transport: Socket for a run that went over NVLink on every channel. The gate already reads the raw NCCL channel lines, which is why it wasn't misled; that stays a rule.

docs.title: ADR 0005: NVSentinel for GPU fault remediation
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: GPU fault detection and remediation, Nordhaven's GPU pools (measured on the Paris L4). Decided after the L4 run, 21 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: When a GPU in Nordhaven's fleet throws a fatal XID, the node has to leave service, its workloads have to move, it has to be repaired and come back, with nobody paged at 3 a.m. Part 1 did this on one L4 with node-problem-detector and a controller I wrote, and the outage it measured (360.9 s) was 83% a lookback timer of mine and 11% a person who hadn't yet run the return-to-service command. Nordhaven runs two GPU types on two providers, so whatever it picks has to know GPU faults, not just node failures, and cost little to operate per pool.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. NVSentinel v1.28.0 NVIDIA's GPU fault pipeline: syslog and DCGM health monitors, quarantine, drain, remediation through a janitor with per-provider back ends, events in MongoDB Knows GPU faults: NVIDIA's XID catalog decides reboot vs GPU reset vs "call support"; DCGM health watches catch faults the kernel log doesn't; the node returns by itself when the monitors report healthy; maintained, released weekly Heavy for one node: MongoDB, cert-manager, seven Deployments and six DaemonSets with every stage on (two of them only for DCGM 3.x or Kata nodes). Its defaults assume a fleet (circuit breaker, a drain that never evicts) and had to be changed here. Weekly releases mean pinning and reading changelogs B. Part 1's controller node-problem-detector turns the XID line into a node condition; 369 lines of Python cordon and evict; a scripted, gated return to service Small, and every line is mine to read; Part 1 tested it (42 tests) and measured it; the return runs dcgmi diag before uncordoning I maintain the XID knowledge; a person runs the return; the five-minute lookback exists only because node-problem-detector replays old kernel lines after a restart; no DCGM path, no reboot or GPU reset C. node-problem-detector, medik8s Node Healthcheck and Self Node Remediation Generic: NPD sets a condition, Node Healthcheck v0.12.0 acts on conditions held for a set duration and hands the node to a remediation template, Self Node Remediation v0.13.0 reboots it in software or through a watchdog, no BMC needed Vendor-neutral, covers every kind of node failure, with a minHealthy/maxUnhealthy guard against remediating half a cluster Knows nothing about GPUs: every XID needs a hand-written NPD rule and a decision about what it means; remediation is node-level only (no GPU reset); conditions must hold for a duration before anything happens (300 s by default), so the timer Part 1 measured comes back by design; no drain policy per namespace

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
NVSentinel, for the GPU pools. Two things decided it. It carries NVIDIA's knowledge of which XID needs what: XID 79 maps to a reboot, others to a GPU reset or to a human, and that's knowledge B and C would make me write and keep current. And it closes the loop with no person in it, which is where Part 1 lost 11% of its outage.

What would change the answer: a provider that already runs medik8s for its CPU fleet would put NVSentinel's GPU knowledge in front of Node Healthcheck rather than run two remediation stacks (NVSentinel's janitor has an external-remediation hook for that). And on a single small node, B is honestly enough; NVSentinel's footprint pays off with a fleet.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Nordhaven now runs MongoDB (Percona, one member here) and cert-manager for its fault pipeline, and NVSentinel's control pods need somewhere to live that isn't a GPU node: in Paris, the CPU worker, which is powered off between uses, so NVSentinel only protects the L4 while that worker is on.
  • The settings I changed are fleet decisions, not demo ones: on a real pool the circuit breaker stays on with an absolute cap, and the drain mode is chosen per namespace.
  • A node comes back without a diagnostic unless post-remediation validation (lifecycle-manager) is turned on. I measured NVSentinel as shipped, so the use case 3 page says what that leaves out.
  • What one L4 can't show: the job can only resume on the node that failed; one simulated XID is not a fleet's fault mix; and the generic reboot is the only remediation exercised, since Scaleway exposes no API NVSentinel's janitor knows.

docs.title: What the L4 run showed
docs.text:
On the Paris L4 on 21 October, with Part 1's job and a SIMULATED XID 79: 288.8 s from fault to resumed training against 360.9 s, goodput 73.0% against 66.4%, and nobody acting at any step. The cordon came 1.3 s after the fault and the drain 1.7 s later. 82% of the outage is now the reboot the XID catalog prescribes (115 s) and the GPU Operator rebuilding the driver (123 s), which Part 1 skipped by handing the GPU back after a diagnostic. A second run through DCGM took 283.3 s, so both detection paths behave the same way. The decision stands; two consequences move up the list:

  • Turn post-remediation validation on before tenants rely on it. The node returned 32 s after the GPU was allocatable, with no diagnostic.
  • A precompiled driver in Paris would remove most of the 123 s; that belongs to the driver decision (ADR 0002).
